National Law No. 11.445/2007, Juiz de Fora Municipal Law No. 14.290/2020, the 2022 Municipal Water and Sanitation Plan, and CESAMA's 2021 Bylaws define water and sewage services around occupied households and building connections, creating legal ambiguity and excluding public spaces from utility mandates. Across five rural communities in Ghana's Wa West District, women and men on Water and Sanitation Management Teams (WSMTs) participate without restriction and formulate borehole operation and maintenance rules by consensus without voting, with women actively initiating rules, conducting routine functionality checks, reporting faults, and contributing event-driven repair fees in some communities (GH₵ 2 for women in Naaha and Ga; GH₵ 1–7 for men across most communities). Outside urbanized zones in the Canton of Lucerne, citizens must self-organize water provision via cooperatives supported by federal and cantonal agricultural subsidies (up to 30% each). In depleted Ward 35 (n = 50), 84% of households relied on private water vendors charging ~$4 per 1,000 L, while 12% could not afford vendors and fetched water from distant municipal wells (>1 km) or informal middlemen, spending >5% of income or hours daily ('water-poor').

Across the Buenos Aires Metropolitan Region (circa 2005), historically rooted institutional fragmentation across 9 official suppliers and 2 regulators (ETOSS and ORAB) yielded stark disparities in coverage and access conditions: AASA served 7.8 million of ~10 million inhabitants with water and 5.8 million with sanitation, compared with 30% served (540,000 of 1.8 million) in AGBA, 850,000 of 2.3 million in ABSA, 60% water (65,000 of 120,000) and 48,000 sanitation in Sudamericana de Aguas (Pilar), and 75% water / 40% sanitation in Marcos Paz (43,400 inhabitants). Within AASA's concession, initial 1993 rules ('user pays' infrastructure charges, limiting service obligation to 'legally urbanised zones' which excluded ~500,000 shanty-town residents, centralized single-technology rules, and single-provider exclusivity) impeded expansion to low-income peripheral areas, whereas subsequent regulatory and contractual adaptations reduced splintering: the 1997 SUMA/CIS cross-subsidy renegotiation lowered average bi-monthly bills for newly connected water users from 60.69 pesos to 15.92 pesos (while increasing already-connected users' bills from 37.26 to 44.52 pesos), and participatory pro-poor schemes (MPG and Agua + Trabajo, alongside 4 to 6.5 peso bi-monthly tariff deductions) connected 520,000 inhabitants of deprived neighbourhoods between 2000 and 2005 (120,000 via MPG and 400,000 via Agua + Trabajo).

Despite State of Public Calamity Decree 0170 of 2016, delayed desalination plant procurement, and late-2018 contract amendment 'Otro Si No. 9' extending Veolia's operation for another 15 years, November 2018 interviews showed no structural change in water access for non-connected and southern/hilly Raizal and low-income neighborhoods, where residents still received piped water only once per month or experienced month-long outages and recurring protests.

Comparative legal-institutional analysis finds that in both Australia and East Timor, modernising statutory water governance reforms subordinate or only superficially engage extant Indigenous and local customary water systems, denying customary uses priority in state water allocation. In Australia, unbundling water from land into tradeable private property entitlements (1994 Water Reform Framework; 2004 National Water Initiative), non-mandatory planning consultation, and narrow interpretations of Native Title Act 1993 rights (restricted to non-exclusive, non-commercial domestic/subsistence uses) have left southern basins nearly wholly allocated to non-Indigenous users and Indigenous-specific water entitlements at less than 0.01% of Australian water diversions (citing Jackson & Langton, 2012), though northern Indigenous advocacy has proposed Strategic Indigenous Reserves (e.g., up to 25% of the consumptive pool in the draft Mataranka Tindal Aquifer Plan). In East Timor, donor-promoted community-managed piped water models struggled where they ignored customary institutions and enforcement sanctions (citing Schoffel, 2006), while state engagement with resurgent customary tara bandu prohibitions and the 2012 Draft Water Resources Law subordinates custom where it conflicts with statutory enforcement, pairs recognition with state ownership and proposed cost-recovery water tariffs, and risks weakening local compliance when state involvement is selective and event-based.

Assessing 14 years (2001–2014) of Free Basic Sanitation (FBSan) implementation in Cape Town's informal settlements, the study finds that failure to achieve universal household sanitation access resulted not solely from municipal maladministration, but from ambiguous national policy definitions, a policy and regulatory vacuum regarding informal settlements and shared/communal sanitation, legal and physical constraints preventing waterborne sewerage or VIP latrines on occupied high-density land, funding gaps (inability to use housing grants in informal areas and unbudgeted O&M/security expenses), inter-departmental silos and restructuring fatigue, officials deferring project-level discretion to avoid personal financial liability under the 1999 Public Finance Management Act, and breakdown of assumed community self-help management.
